body_markdown:
Just as I’d hoped, the readers of Hagerty Media are no strangers to taking a long road trip. Because[when we asked you](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/what-was-your-longest-road-trip/comment-page-5/#comments) for your longest road trip, we received pages and pages of stories. The only problem is that we cannot republish all of them for *According To You* , so I highly recommend you visit those comments to read them all.


But for now, have a look at these selections, as I am sure you will love the stories presented by your fellow readers as they traveled by car, truck, and even motorcycle!


## International Travel


James Moy Photography/Getty Images


**Ken G:** Myself and my wife drove 24,000 kilometers around Australia in six weeks. I was recovering from a dose of the flu, we had a 1600-cc Suzuki ute with a canopy. The top speed was 105 kph (65 mph), except when we got behind a big coach that sucked us up to 120. I was 35 then, and I swear I looked older then than I do now at 72.


**Ethan G:** I went on a Europe road trip in my 2017 F56 Cooper S, first traveling to Belgium to stay in Malmedy for the European Le Mans series at Spa, as well visiting the Nürburgring for some hot laps. After this I drove down through Germany, even got the chance to drive an autobahn toward Switzerland, where I stayed for a week and took the opportunity to drive Klausen Pass and Furka pass, then drove further south into Italy through the Splügen Pass to head for Lake Como.


After my two-week stay in Italy, I headed back to the U.K., driving through Switzerland and France. All in all, the whole trip covered 2600 miles.


**Rick:** Longest road trip was two of us on motorcycles: Seattle to Prince George, BC, then across Canada Highway 1 to Montreal. Then headed south to Raleigh, North Carolina, then over to Louisville, Kansas City, Denver, Spokane, and back to Seattle. Roughly 8000 miles in 21 days—those were the days!


**Geordie:** My longest trip was a 23,000-mile circumnavigation of the U.S. and Canada in a 1961 Vauxhall Victor station wagon. Two of us were doing research for our architecture theses, and the four of us were sightseeing. We hit 37 states and six provinces in 10 weeks, camping most nights.


**Tom P:** Back in the mid-1970s, I drove my nearly-new 1974 MGB roadster from Quebec City to Vancouver. I was on my own and spent six days on the road. Loved every minute of it. I still have the B, 50 years on.


**Jim C:** In 1969, two buddies and I drove a VW bus from the Chicago area to Acapulco and back. Guessing about 2500 miles each way. Unforgettable trip.


**GC:** Minnesota to Acapulco and back in a ’63 Ford Fairlane in 1968, prior to my induction into the Navy. I remember a bartender in Taxco remarking that “I’m Mexican and I wouldn’t do that,” but we were young and stupid and the world was a different place.


## A Surprising Number of Miatas


Tyler Houts


**John D:** Wichita Falls, Texas, to various places on my way to Olympic National Park in Washington, Crater Lake, Zion National Park, and back to my starting point. A little over 6000 miles in three weeks. In an NA Miata, tent camping all the way. Miata is the answer.


**Mike L:** I’ve put thousands of miles on my Miatas (NA, NB, NC, and ND) on road trips. My wife and I took our honeymoon in my NB with 2000-plus- mile road trip from St. Louis to Upper Michigan, looping around Lake Michigan. Also, 2000-plus miles twice from St. Louis to Springfield, Massachusetts—once in my NA and once in my NB.


**Desmond G:** I drove my NA Miata solo from Dallas to Somis, California, when I moved back out here. Years later I would match that trip when my dad gave me his old Suburban, but that time it was a family road trip with my folks joining me.


## Route 66 Love


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


**Donald K:** Three couples, we each drove our own ’39 Chevys and a ’46 Chevy pickup from Champaign, Illinois, to California on Route 66. We had a wonderful time as we stopped when someone wanted to see something, even if it wasn’t on 66. Once we got to California, we drove on Highway 1 to Seattle and stayed for a week.


We ate seafood and played golf all week. Went home through the Upper Midwest with a stop at Little Big Horn. And got home after 22-or-so days on the road. No breakdowns driving old hot rods.


## A Lot of Alaska


Nathan Petroelje


**Greg E:** I’ve done several cross-country trips from the West Coast to the East Coast. But the weirdest and maybe longest (seemed at the time) was when myself and four other 19-year-old idiots piled into a $235 ’62 Chevy wagon and drove from southern Oregon to Fairbanks, Alaska. It was in March of ’75 and 25 below zero. Being poor kids, we all slept in the car at night in our arctic gear. It took us 5.5 days, and this was all to get jobs on the Alaskan oil pipeline.


**Larry M:** Summer trip to Alaska pulling a travel trailer. 18,000 miles for truck, 12,000 miles on trailer.


**RBMojo:** Four lads from Tulsa drove a reconstituted ’63 Comet wagon (updated the six-cylinder to a 302 Mustang V-8, trans, and front end) from Tulsa to Anchorage and back in the summer of 1978. An epic two-week adventure. The ALCAN was still gravel, with all the pitfalls of tire wear, rocks thrown by trucks, etc. Picked up a hitchhiker along the way (an e-Canada bond trader) and deposited him at a bar in Alaska where he was taking possession of a cabin in the mountains sight-unseen… only optimistic young men need apply!


**Rocco417:** My brother and myself left St. Louis in a 1974 Ford F250. We were planning on going west and then up to the ALCAN highway. Well, we made it west to Cali and up the coast to Seattle. We had hit every national park and KOA along the way, but found out two things: America is a big country, and money we had didn’t go far.


After Seattle, funds were running low so the ALCAN was out. We headed back east through Idaho, Wyoming, etc. nonstop. What a trip, I will never forget the things we did, the beauty we saw, or the people we met.


**Joe S:** Around 1980, I was living in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. I drove to Seattle, picked up a buddy who flew in from New York, drove to Alaska and around as much as we could. Then down to San Fransisco, where my buddy flew back home. I continued back to Michigan.


This took a little less than four weeks, and I seem to remember about 12,000 miles. It was February, and the car was a 1974 Opel station wagon. Looking back, we had to be total idiots to pull this off.


**Alan S:** If motorcycles count, from Florida to the Arctic Circle and back. If four wheelers, from Florida to Hyder, Alasksa, then return via Oregon, Pacific Coast Highway, etc.


## America, the Beautiful


Library of Congress


**Edwin G:** 6000 miles from Tampa Bay through the Midwest, North Dakota, Wyoming, Colorado, and back through northern Texas and the South. We take a 3000–5000-mile trip every late summer and have for 10 years.


**Tim:** A relocation from the west to the east had us on a 4000-mile trip I planned through 17 states. The fastest route would have been only 2200 miles and nine states, but who goes on a road trip just to get from Point A to Point B?


While planning the trip, I specifically looked for interesting stops every couple of hours, with no more than six hours of driving on the longest days. Sometimes the stops were silly diversions, (“Who wants to see the Jolly Green Giant?”), but there were plenty of epic destinations, such as the Henry Ford Museum and River Rouge factory tour. In the end, though the trip was long, we were not travel weary, and the whole family agreed it was fun and worthwhile. We made a photo book that captured the memories and titled it, “The Great American Road Trip.”


**jacob g:** I went to college at Michigan Technological University, which for those who don’t know is in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. North of there, in the little town of Copper Harbor, is the starting spot of U.S. Highway 41. It runs from there all the way to Miami, a nearly 2000-mile one-way trip. So, my friends and I decided we wanted to road-trip from Copper Harbor to Miami and back, staying on U.S. 41 as strictly as we could, driving non-stop and rotating drivers every four hours, when we would take a rest stop of about 10–15 minutes.


Took nearly four days, with us all eating and sleeping in the vehicle (my ’98 Plymouth Grand Voyager was the chariot for the five of us). It was 4000-ish miles of restless, cramped, and, by the end, extremely B.O.-smelling adventure!


**wentwest:** A road trip that wasn’t really a pleasure was a journey we took on 9/13/2001, from Oakland to Chatham, Massachusetts. A young member of our extended family was getting married on 9/15, and we were supposed to fly there, but the 9/11 attacks changed the rules.


Nothing was flying. There were four of us, so we rented a minivan, loaded up at 6 a.m. on the 13th, and hit the road: I-80 to Chicago, then I-90 to Boston, then down to the Cape. Sea to shining sea in about 50 hours. We stopped for gas, bathrooms, and then headed out, driving in three-hour shifts. We ate the food we had brought from our house. We arrived at about 11 a.m. on the 15th, took quick showers and made it to the wedding.


Lots of stories and very short chats at gas stations with other Americans trying to get home. It was interesting and tedious. There was a massive train wreck in Nevada, close to the highway, but it never made the news.


Touring Club Italiano/Marka/Universal Images Group via Getty Images


**Mike H:** In 1972, the Army was moving me from my ROTC assignment in Cheney, Washington (eastern WA) to Ft. Belvoir, Virginia. We packed the 1971 Alfa Romeo Berlina trunk with grocery bags full of our clothes. Pillows and blankets filled the area between the front and back seats so that the two babies and one dog had a level place to play and sleep. Instead of heading east, we went west to the mouth of the Columbia River then headed south on whatever highway was closest to the coast.


We stopped in San Francisco, then it was on to Monterey so I could be on the pit crew for an SCCA B Production GT350, then watch the Can-Am race at Laguna Seca. After the race, we headed east, stopped to see an Army buddy in Missouri, and reached Ft. Belvoir in 19 days. It was quite a trip. Sadly, the kids don’t remember it.


**Mike S:** In 2019, my wife and her bestie planned a jaunt (by air) to Charleston, South Carolina, to look at houses and stuff. I begged off and said I’d rather take a solo trip across the U.S. on the blue highways, i.e., no interstate roads.


And I did. Took Highway 2 from its beginning in Washington, through Idaho, Montana, Minnesota (jumped across the Mississippi River at its source, spent a few days in Duluth exploring Lake Superior), then to the Soo Locks, where Highway 2 ends.


Down around Toledo, up to Niagara Falls, then down to Maryland, dipped a toe in Delaware’s Atlantic Ocean, then back through the middle of the country and home to Vancouver, WA. Took 28 days, met a lot of interesting people, and had a great time.


I drove my then-almost-new Subaru Crosstrek, figuring I’d probably hate it by trip’s end, but ended up liking it even more. 6134 miles, averaged 32.3 mpg.


I’d do it again.


Andrew Newton


**Hugh W:** Newport, Rhode Island, to Sacramento in a 1971 Triumph TR6.


**jjd1010:** 19,950 miles in 1986. Had a six-month sabbatical from work, so we bought a used RV, got all the maps and guidebooks offered by AAA, loaded our two preschool kids in the RV, and pulled out of our driveway in Massachusetts.


We had no plan other than wanting to visit national parks and to stay off the interstate highways. We criss-crossed our way down the eastern part of America until the road ended in Key West. Then we did the same thing to all four corners of America, crossing into the Rockies probably seven or eight times. Six months and 3165 gallons of gas later, we pulled into our driveway back in Massachusetts. America the beautiful!


**James G:** Miami to the Grand Canyon, camping in a Porsche 914. Over dinner at the El Tovar Lodge, on our wedding anniversary, my wife told me she was pregnant with our first child.


**John R:** Over 21,500 miles during a seven-month excursion, starting with Route 66 and then just staying on the road, starting in May of last year. Having a 20-year-old Class B motorhome helps, and I stayed at Harvest Host and Boondocker sites and Cracker Barrel restaurants. I watched the weather forecast and zig-zagged around the country taking in museums, national parks and state parks. I helped out with a bit of volunteer work for museums and enjoyed the people and local characteristics of our vast country!


**JonMo** : In 2004, my buddy and I drove his Volvo 850 station wagon from Newton, Massachusetts, to visit our girlfriends in Austin, Texas, and Greensboro, North Carolina, before returning home. We stopped along the way for fishing, a factory tour, and to visit national parks. It was a great way to spend a few weeks. We totaled a tick under 4000 miles. The Volvo held up great, even in the face of the worst hailstorm I’ve ever witnessed.


Chevrolet


**Lee Craner:** August 1997, Orlando to Southern California in a 1971 Corvette.


No issues whatsoever. Great trip.
